clue.text: One old railway charity

parts.note: a means one
the London, Midland and Scottish Railway, merged into British Railways in 1948

explanation.surface: A defunct railway line kept going as a charitable concern.
explanation.definitionFit: Alms are gifts of money or food given to the poor, which is charity in its oldest sense.

clue.text: Delicate stroke beheaded king and cavalryman

indicators.note: losing its head, the word drops its first letter

parts.note: a glance is a delicate deflecting shot in cricket, here without its first letter
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A king is beheaded with a deft blow, and so is a horse soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a king beheaded, but it is the stroke that loses its head: a glance is a deft cricket shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A lancer is a mounted soldier who originally fought armed with a lance.

clue.text: One serviced both Chatterleys' venery

parts.note: surface reading: a man who satisfied the sexual appetites of Lord and Lady Chatterley
setter's reading: venery also means hunting, so this is the estate employee who kept the game for the Chatterleys

explanation.walkthrough: In D. H. Lawrence's novel, Mellors looks after Sir Clifford's game and becomes Lady Chatterley's lover; venery means both hunting and sexual indulgence.
explanation.definitionFit: Mellors is employed to rear and protect birds for shooting on the Chatterley estate, serving its hunting.

clue.text: Picked up skins one having dropped off

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking something up lifts it so it reads from the bottom upward

parts.note: to peel fruit is to skin it
a means one

explanation.surface: Someone collected the skins that one person shed.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop off is an idiom for falling into slumber, so someone who has dropped off is sleeping.

clue.text: Get on with old Shakespearean character

parts.note: to get on in life is to prosper
O is the usual abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Advice to get along with an old figure from Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero is the exiled magician-duke at the centre of The Tempest.

clue.text: Base of Vulcan fleet navy retains

indicators.note: the phrase retains, or keeps within it, a run of consecutive letters

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: The base of a Vulcan bomber is held by a naval fleet.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vulcan was a British nuclear bomber, suggesting an airbase; the setter means the Roman god of fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Myth placed the smithy of the fire god beneath the Sicilian volcano, so it served as his workshop.

clue.text: Old reform movement out of time has a special attractiveness

indicators.note: out of means taken away from, so something is removed

parts.note: Chartism, the 1830s-40s British working-class campaign for political reform, minus T
taken as written
T, abbreviation for time, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A historic reform campaign, past its time, keeps a certain allure.
explanation.definitionFit: Charisma is a compelling personal charm that draws others in, an unusual magnetism.

clue.text: Take out capo perhaps and keep protection

parts.note: to draw a weapon or a card is to take it out
a capo is a movable bar clamped across a guitar's strings, a kind of bridge

explanation.surface: Kill the Mafia boss and keep the protection money.
explanation.walkthrough: Take out and capo point to a mob hit; the capo here is the guitarist's clamp. A keep is a castle's central tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A raisable bridge over a moat guards a castle's entrance, defending the stronghold against attackers.

clue.text: A shopping centre rejected unorthodox source of wool

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the phrase before it is read from the end

parts.note: taken as written
a mall is a covered shopping centre

explanation.surface: A shopping mall turns away some unconventional supplier of wool.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheep are the usual providers of fleece; this South American camelid is a less conventional one.

clue.text: What carries the injured needing time on emergency room

parts.note: a stretch is a period, especially a prison term
ER is the usual abbreviation for an emergency room; 'on' puts it after

explanation.surface: An ambulance crew needs time to reach the hospital's casualty department.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretcher is the portable frame on which wounded or sick people are moved lying down.

clue.text: Salmon? Scotland's foremost certainly as Jock would say

indicators.note: foremost picks out the leading letter of the word it follows

parts.note: first letter of the country's name

indicators.note: a Scotsman's spoken phrase is to be heard rather than spelt out

parts.note: 'och aye' is the stereotypical Scots for 'oh yes', certainly

explanation.surface: A Scotsman, asked about salmon, says 'och aye' with great certainty.
explanation.walkthrough: Jock is a traditional nickname for a Scotsman. The question mark warns that the definition is an example: this is one species of salmon.
explanation.definitionFit: The sockeye is a red-fleshed Pacific species, so it is one particular kind of that fish.

clue.text: Who killed Robin in bar brawl

parts.note: a spar is a pole or bar
a row is a noisy quarrel or brawl

explanation.surface: A man called Robin was killed in a pub fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a murder in a pub, but the nursery rhyme answers 'Who killed Cock Robin?' with 'I, said the Sparrow'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old nursery rhyme this small bird confesses to shooting Cock Robin with its bow and arrow.

clue.text: Soup, unadulterated, with natural base

parts.note: unadulterated means pure, with nothing mixed in
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A soup made from wholesome, unadulterated ingredients with a natural stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natural base' sounds like stock for the soup; in mathematics it is the constant e, the base of natural logarithms.
explanation.definitionFit: A purée is a smooth blended food, and thick vegetable soups are often served as one.

clue.text: Nuts — this is a cop out

indicators.note: out suggests things put out of order, so the preceding letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Calling something a cop-out is crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like an exclamation of disbelief, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pistachios are the green-kerneled seeds of a Middle Eastern tree, eaten as snacks.

clue.text: Herald comes round again, endlessly left outside

indicators.note: without its end, the word loses its final letter
one piece placed outside wraps around the other phrase

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship, losing its last letter
something that recurs comes round again

explanation.surface: A messenger returns once more, with someone left standing outside.
explanation.walkthrough: Port is the nautical word for left, the side of a ship facing forward on the left.
explanation.definitionFit: A precursor goes before and announces something to come, just as a herald foreshadows an arrival.

clue.text: Give emphasis in category of music

parts.note: a book filed under a heading is in that category
a score is written music

explanation.surface: Stress something within a particular genre of music.
explanation.definitionFit: To underscore a point is to highlight or stress it, as if drawing a line beneath it.

clue.text: What's lucky at wedding …… it moves with the times

parts.note: a chimney sweep at a wedding is a traditional good-luck charm
a clock's second hand moves round as the time passes

explanation.surface: Wedding good-luck customs are traditions that change with the times.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half does double duty: it gives the last two words and defines the whole, the continuously moving seconds pointer on a clock or watch.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweep second hand glides round the dial continuously, keeping pace with passing time.

clue.text: One no longer loved stout trader

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
porter is a dark beer like stout

explanation.surface: A former lover is a portly merchant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' reads as describing a plump trader, but it is the dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: An exporter is a merchant who sells goods abroad, a kind of overseas dealer.

clue.text: This person is dividing property rate

indicators.note: something dividing another sits in its middle, splitting it into two parts

parts.note: an estate is landed property
the setter speaking: I am, shortened to I'm

explanation.surface: The speaker is splitting up an estate and assessing the local property tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Property rate' looks like a tax; the two words have separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate something is to judge or assess its value, which is what estimating does.

clue.text: Like robbers, gives stress to hotel

parts.note: as means in the manner of, like
pirates are robbers at sea

explanation.surface: Robbers put a hotel under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: To aspirate is to sound the letter h: someone who says 'hotel' rather than 'an 'otel' gives the h its breath.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirating a word means pronouncing its initial h with a puff of breath, emphasising that letter.

clue.text: Mow down heavily armed police with high explosive

parts.note: a SWAT team is an armed police tactical unit
HE is the standard abbreviation for high explosive

explanation.surface: Armed police with explosives cut down their targets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mow down' suggests a massacre, but it is the farming sense: a swathe is the strip cut by a scythe.
explanation.definitionFit: Swathing is cutting grass or crops in broad strips, the way a mower works across a field.

clue.text: Lee's drinking companion reared around inn primarily

indicators.note: around says one piece is wrapped about the other

parts.note: reared up means rose

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letter of the word before it

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A man called Lee has a drinking partner who rose up near the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurie Lee's memoir is 'Cider with Rosie', so Rosie is the companion he drank with.
explanation.definitionFit: In Laurie Lee's famous memoir, Rosie is the girl who shares cider with him under a hay wagon.

clue.text: See lofted shot going round bunker

indicators.note: going round means circling another piece, enclosing it

parts.note: a skier is a ball hit high into the air, especially in cricket
v stands for vide, Latin for see

explanation.surface: A golfer watches a high shot clear a sand trap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunker' looks like golf, but it is someone who bunks off, skipping school or work.
explanation.definitionFit: A skiver dodges work or school, and to bunk off is British slang for the same truancy.

clue.text: Feature shown by Oliver, say, could be moreish

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters that follow might be rearranged into something else

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something about Oliver could be described as moreish.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist bravely asked for more gruel, so 'moreish' is a fitting source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking the workhouse master for a second helping was an act of great courage and boldness.

clue.text: Naughty children in The Simpsons

indicators.note: in says the letters are sitting inside the following word

parts.note: the run of letters after its first

explanation.surface: Bart and friends are the badly behaved kids in the cartoon.
explanation.definitionFit: Imps are mischievous little sprites, so the word is used for mischievous youngsters.

clue.text: Invite bids for uranium in case

indicators.note: in places one item inside the other

parts.note: a case at law is an action
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: Someone puts a case of uranium up for sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like a box holding the uranium, but it is a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: To auction something is to sell it publicly, inviting buyers to make offers.

clue.text: Festival when French emperor's not half upset

indicators.note: not half means half the word is left off
in a down clue, upset tips the word over so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: Napoleon without its first half

explanation.surface: A celebration at which Napoleon was not entirely pleased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' sounds like British slang for very, but it means half the name is missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel is another word for Christmas, the winter feast celebrating the Nativity.

clue.text: Deliver bad ball — batter hit cover point's head

indicators.note: to batter is to pound out of shape, so the letters get beaten into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: head is the top or first letter of the word before it

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bowler sends down a poor ball, and the batter hits it over the fielder at cover point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' reads as the batsman but is the anagram signal. Cover point is a cricket fielding position.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, to overpitch is to bowl a ball too full, landing it so close the batsman can drive easily.

clue.text: He had a tale to tell about first lady

definitions.text: He had a tale to tell

parts.note: re means about, concerning
Eve was the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: A man had a story to tell concerning a president's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims each tell a tale, one being the Reeve's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The Reeve, an estate steward, is one of Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims and narrates his own story.
